drills.q: Explain what changed and what didn't when Vertex AI Agent Builder became Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform in April 2026.
drills.a: Changed: console hierarchy inverted (agents first-class, training/AutoML/Endpoints now sub-features), Agent Builder + Agentspace absorbed into one namespace, A2A v1.0 became the default interoperability layer, Agent Studio (low-code) and Agent Gateway added, 'Vertex AI' label removed from console as of 2026-05-21. Unchanged: underlying APIs, SDKs, and billing for existing Model Registry/training/Endpoints workloads -- no breaking changes for current deployments. It's an organizational/console-level rebrand, not a rewrite.

drills.q: A team's Vertex AI bill doesn't drop after a demo project ends and traffic goes to zero. Diagnose and give the fix.
drills.a: Deployed models bill per hour for reserved serving capacity regardless of whether prediction requests arrive -- traffic dropping to zero doesn't stop the charge, only explicitly undeploying the model from the endpoint does. Fix: build undeploy into project teardown process, track deployed endpoints against active projects, and alert on endpoints with zero traffic for N days rather than relying on someone remembering to undeploy manually.

drills.q: Design a cost-conscious architecture for a high-volume (millions/day) support-ticket classification agent using Gemini models, naming every cost lever.
drills.a: Use Flash or Flash-Lite (not Pro) for the base classification task -- no frontier reasoning needed, ~10-20x cheaper per token than Pro. Escalate only genuinely ambiguous cases to Pro rather than running every call through the expensive tier. Batch API (flat 50% off, 24hr SLA) for anything tolerating delay, e.g. end-of-day reclassification/audit. Context caching for any shared system prompt or reused knowledge-base excerpt. Retrieve only relevant snippets via Vector Search rather than stuffing a full knowledge base into context, keeping calls under the 200K-token long-context surcharge threshold.

drills.q: Distinguish Agent Engine's Sessions from Memory Bank, and describe a concrete production bug from conflating them.
drills.a: Sessions: short-term, chronological history within one conversation, giving contextual continuity across requests in that conversation only. Memory Bank (GA early 2026): long-term, extracts salient facts across sessions for cross-session retrieval. Bug: an agent relying only on Session history 'forgets' a fact a user stated three conversations ago (e.g. a dietary restriction), because that fact was never extracted into Memory Bank -- each new session starts blind to prior sessions' content unless Memory Bank is explicitly enabled and populated.

drills.q: A team is choosing between Vector Search and AlloyDB AI's built-in ScaNN index for a RAG system with ~500K document chunks. Walk through the decision and the tradeoff.
drills.a: 500K vectors sits comfortably within range where an operational database's built-in vector index performs well without needing purpose-built billion-scale ANN architecture. If the data already needs to live in AlloyDB for transactional reasons, colocating the vector index avoids standing up a second separately-billed system (Vector Search bills per-node-hour regardless of traffic). Vector Search becomes the better call once scale grows toward millions-to-billions of vectors or QPS exceeds what one operational instance's vector index can serve alongside transactional load -- 'always use the specialized tool' is a reflexive answer, not an evaluated tradeoff.

drills.q: Explain the difference between Vector Search's brute-force and tree-AH index types, and when brute force in production is a mistake.
drills.a: Brute force: exact linear search, no tunable parameters -- correct but latency scales linearly with dataset size, appropriate only for small datasets or ground-truth baseline validation. Tree-AH (ANN, ScaNN-based): trades ~1% recall for sub-10ms latency even at billion-vector scale. Using brute force in production at real scale is a mistake because a system fine at 10K vectors becomes unacceptably slow at 10M with no configuration knob available to fix it -- brute force has zero tunable parameters to trade off.

drills.q: Compare AgentCore's and ADK's architectural philosophies and state when each fits better.
drills.a: AgentCore ships Runtime, Memory, Identity, Gateway, and Policy as separately composable services -- suits teams wanting fine-grained control, e.g. swapping in a custom identity provider or using only Gateway. ADK is a code-first, opinionated framework (Agent, tools, workflow graph) deploying as a unit to Agent Engine -- faster to get a working multi-agent system running, less flexibility to swap individual runtime pieces. Fast time-to-working-agent with GCP-native data integration (BigQuery, Vector Search) fits ADK; fine-grained independently-swappable primitives for complex zero-trust/multi-tenant deployment fits AgentCore.

drills.q: A candidate claims A2A and MCP solve the same problem so you only need one. Correct this precisely.
drills.a: They operate at different layers. MCP standardizes agent-to-TOOL communication -- how an agent/model calls external tools and data sources. A2A standardizes agent-to-AGENT communication -- task delegation, status reporting, and artifact exchange between independent peer agents, a fundamentally different integration surface. A real system commonly uses both: MCP for an agent's own tool calls, A2A to delegate part of a task to a genuinely separate agent. Wrapping another agent as an MCP tool works for a crude one-shot handoff but loses A2A's purpose-built semantics for ongoing task lifecycle and streaming status.

drills.q: Why does the Gemini API's 200K-token long-context surcharge threshold matter for RAG-vs-long-context architecture decisions?
drills.a: Gemini 3.1 Pro's price rises from $2.00/$12.00 per 1M input/output tokens under 200K to $2.50/$15.00 above it -- every call using more than 200K tokens pays the higher rate for the ENTIRE call, not just the excess. For workloads with large, mostly-static documents queried repeatedly, chunking and retrieving only relevant portions via RAG (keeping most calls under 200K tokens) is cheaper per call than relying on the full 2M-token window every time, plus retrieval generally beats long-context recall precision for finding specific facts in very long documents.

drills.q: Justify choosing Azure AI Foundry over Gemini Enterprise or Bedrock for a specific customer, and state what would make that choice wrong.
drills.a: Foundry is the strongest choice for an org whose workflows already run heavily through Microsoft 365 -- one-click Teams deployment and native Exchange/SharePoint/Graph integration genuinely compress time-to-value to days for that specific org shape. It would be wrong for a GCP-native org with data concentrated in BigQuery/Spanner (Gemini Enterprise's tighter data-platform integration wins) or an AWS-native org needing AgentCore's modular zero-trust/multi-tenant primitives. Model access alone (e.g. OpenAI models via Foundry) doesn't outweigh integration cost -- a GCP-native team adopting Foundry purely for model choice takes on real multi-cloud egress/identity-federation overhead a same-cloud platform avoids.

drills.q: A team is migrating a working LangChain prototype to ADK/Agent Engine. Should they do a full rewrite? Explain the judgment call.
drills.a: Not necessarily -- ADK is explicitly model-agnostic and deployment-agnostic so teams aren't forced into all-or-nothing migration. A team with working, battle-tested LangChain tool integrations can keep those components and adopt ADK/Agent Engine specifically for pieces that add clear value (managed session/memory persistence, GCP-native scaling) rather than rewriting working code for its own sake. The tradeoff to name explicitly: a mixed stack won't get Agent Engine's full managed-scaling/observability story for the non-ADK components -- that's a real cost, not something to gloss over, and the decision should weigh migration cost against incremental benefit per component, not assume a full rewrite is automatically justified because a new platform launched.

drills.q: Explain why picking an agent platform based purely on model-quality benchmarks is an incomplete evaluation.
drills.a: All three major clouds now carry near-frontier models from multiple vendors via their catalogs (Model Garden covers Gemini/Claude/Llama/Mistral; Bedrock covers Claude/Titan/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/DeepSeek; Foundry covers OpenAI plus a broader catalog) -- model quality is decreasingly a differentiator since the same top models are often available on more than one platform. The actual differentiator is the surrounding runtime/memory/identity/tool-access architecture and fit with the org's existing cloud footprint -- e.g. Foundry's measurable M365 integration advantage for Microsoft-centric orgs has nothing to do with any model's benchmark score.
